To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) U(VI) is incorporated in hematite as U(VI) uranate; (2) U(VI), incorporated in hematite, was reduced to U V; (3) U(V), incorporated in hematites, was stable at Eh -0.28 to +0.21 and pH 7-8 for up to 5 week; and (4) U(IV) was not detected in the hematite structure at any of the conditions tested.

(1) U(V) is a stable oxidation state in hematite under circumneutral pH conditions, and (2) U(V) was formed by reduction of U(VI), incorporated in the structure, and not by reduction of U(IV), non-incorporated in the structure, of hematite.
U(V) is the stable oxidation state of uranium incorporated into the structure of hematites at pH 7 and Eh -0.3 to -0.2 V.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the stability of different uranium redox states in the presence of hematite.
the stability of U(V) in hematite, and we show that U(V) can be formed in the presence of a reductant and at Eh conditions that are lower than those previously reported for U(IV) formation.
the stability of U(V) and the mechanism of U(VI)/U(IV) reduction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
U(V) is stable in uranate environments in hematite, whereas U(VI) and U(IV) are stable in uranates in hematite and in non-incorporated uranyl species, respectively.
the U(IV) stability field is not extended to the Eh-pH conditions of the present experiment and, thus, U(VI) reduction is not inhibited by uranate coordination in hematite.
the reduction of U(VI), incorporated in hematite, is not a simple two-electron process, and that U(IV) can be stabilized in the structure by the presence of U(V).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
uranate coordination of U(VI), which is incorporated in the structure, is more resistant to reduction than U(VI) not incorporated in the structure.
the stability of U(V) in hematite is increased by its incorporation in the structure, and that the stability of uranate is enhanced in hematite relative to aqueous solution.
U(VI) is stable in hematite under reducing conditions, but is reduced to U(V) and/or U(IV) at more positive redox potentials.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the oxidation state of uranium incorporated in hematite can be controlled by the redox conditions of the system.
the stability field for U(V) in hematite is significantly wider than previously thought.
the oxidation state of uranium is not only controlled by redox potential but also by the coordination environment and the structure in which it resides.
